intro: Lesson 9: The four schools of fiqh. Read the ideas from the lesson, then do the tasks.

panels.title: Why schools developed
points: Different ways of understanding the evidence

blocks.answers: Abu Hanifah: d. 150 AH, Kufa; the Hanafi school grew from his circle. Malik: d. 179 AH, Madinah; wrote al-Muwatta'; taught ash-Shafi'i. Ash-Shafi'i: d. 204 AH, Iraq and Egypt; studied with Malik; taught Ahmad. Ahmad: d. 241 AH, Baghdad; compiled al-Musnad. In common: they followed the Qur'an and Sunnah and respected each other.

keywords.def: here: a great scholar who founded a school
a scholar's careful effort to reach a ruling from the evidence

questions.q: Explain two reasons why the four schools developed.
questions.a: Hadith reached different cities at different times, and scholars understood words and evidence differently through ijtihad.

questions.q: Imam profile cards on the pupil PDF (four cards: name, dates, city, teacher or student, one famous book or fact), then one sentence on what they had in common.
questions.a: Accurate cards (e.g. Malik: al-Muwatta'; Ahmad: al-Musnad); common: following the Qur'an and Sunnah

questions.q: Extend: why is ijtihad only for qualified scholars?
questions.a: It needs deep knowledge of Arabic, the Qur'an, Sunnah and principles.

questions.q: Stretch: which school is most followed in your family or community, and where is it common worldwide?
questions.a: Pupils' own; e.g. Hanafi in South Asia and Turkey, Shafi'i in East Africa and South-East Asia
A) Ash-Shafi'i. Ahmad studied with ash-Shafi'i; ash-Shafi'i studied with Malik.

questions.q: Think again: can experts differ and all be respected?
questions.a: Yes, when they follow evidence honestly, like the four imams.
